Chapter
	IV
OVER	HILL	AND	UNDER	HILL
There	were	many	paths	that	led	up	into	those	mountains,
and	many	passes	over	them.	But	most	of	the	paths	were
cheats	 and	 deceptions	 and	 led	 nowhere	 or	 to	 bad	 ends;
and	 most	 of	 the	 passes	 were	 infested	 by	 evil	 things	 and
dreadful	dangers.	The	dwarves	and	the	hobbit,	helped	by
the	wise	advice	of	Elrond	and	the	knowledge	and	memory
of	Gandalf,	took	the	right	road	to	the	right	pass.
Long	days	after	they	had	climbed	out	of	the	valley	and
left	the	Last	Homely	House	miles	behind,	they	were	still
going	 up	 and	 up	 and	 up.	 It	 was	 a	 hard	 path	 and	 a
dangerous	path,	a	crooked	way	and	a	lonely	and	a	long.
Now	 they	 could	 look	 back	 over	 the	 lands	 they	 had	 left,
laid	out	behind	them	far	below.	Far,	far	away	in	the	West,
where	 things	 were	 blue	 and	 faint,	 Bilbo	 knew	 there	 lay
his	own	country	of	safe	and	comfortable	things,	and	his
little	hobbit-hole.	He	shivered.	It	was	getting	bitter	cold
up	 here,	 and	 the	 wind	 came	 shrill	 among	 the	 rocks.
Boulders,	 too,	 at	 times	 came	 galloping	 down	 the
mountain-sides,	let	loose	by	mid-day	sun	upon	the	snow,
and	passed	among	them	(which	was	lucky),	or	over	their
heads	(which	was	alarming).	The	nights	were	comfortless
and	chill,	and	they	did	not	dare	to	sing	or	talk	too	loud,
